title: “Obey the inscrutable exhortations of your soul” won
summary:
The stickiest line to come out of this whole mini-canon is Yatharth’s: “you cannot live defending your soul in a court of law.” It’s the moment the meme stops being cute Calvin & Hobbes energy and becomes a real critique of living by external rubrics—ratings, status, “show me proof,” whatever—when the thing you’re trying to protect is basically pre-verbal.

The thread’s origin is @visakanv doing his usual “references I use pretty often” curation and dropping item #24: “consider obeying the inscrutable exhortations of your soul,” then immediately linking the Calvin & Hobbes strip (“stop and smell the flowers”) where Type A turns even flower-smelling into a competitive trophy (“Flower Smelling Champion”). People start using it as a permission slip. @AskYatharth turns it into practice: if you don’t know what your “exhortations” are, “that makes it a lot easier… then you just go try them” (grab the keys, take the midnight drive; you learn by motion, not deliberation). The peak “tension” beat is his crush story: he feels forced to translate his subjective awe into a conventional 1–10 scale to make it defensible, realizes that’s the soul getting crushed, and chooses to invite people into his experience instead of litigating it. 

After that, it spreads as a general-purpose tool: @Malcolm_Ocean riffs that obeying your soul is the non-bullshit version of “God’s favor” as a status explanation; @QiaochuYuan uses it as life advice (“at any age”); @slimepriestess reframes identity as acting on a feeling you can’t justify except “i’m casting a spell.” Then Visa escalates it into a broader worldview: the “heart laser” people who simply like what they like are compelling, and having a clear vision feels like a “sickening advantage” over social-consensus navigation; hero-worship Qs (“what would you ask Steve Jobs?”) become a way to hide from your own discernment. It never really “dies”—it just periodically resurfaces (by 2025 @scottdomes reposts the original comic like a completed circle). Why care: it’s a surprisingly sharp diagnostic for when you’re optimizing for approval vs. actually steering your life, and it gives you an excuse—almost a mandate—to move first and explain later.
